docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
• The development of a shared ontology enables interoperability between Common Core Ontologies (CCO) and OGC EDR.
  • The shared ontology takes into consideration various mappings between the two representations (CCO and EDR) by identifying BroaderThan, NarrowerThan, Similar, etc. relationships between the concepts in the two representations as well as the properties.
  • Subsequently the bridge concepts between them are identified and used in the alignment of the two representations by the shared ontology, which is developed in OWL.
  • A SHACL (Shape Constraint Language) shape is developed for validating RDF data against a set of constraints. To create a SHACL shape for the shared ontology, we define constraints for classes, properties, and individuals.
  • Finally, the usefulness of the developed shared ontology has been demonstrated in two use cases using SPARQL.

docs.title: Technical Implementation
docs.text:
CCO provides a broader and more general ontology for modeling entities, processes, qualities, and relationships, making it suitable for semantic interoperability across domains.

EDR is narrower and focuses specifically on environmental data retrieval through APIs, with concepts.

Table 1 provides a mapping between CCO and OGC EDR showing the BroderThan, NarrowerThan and similar concepts

docs.title: Table 1. Comprehensive Mapping between CCO and OGC EDR
docs.text: Category CCO Concept/Property EDR Concept/Property Relationship Remarks Core Entities Object cco:Object Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models physical and abstract objects. Physical Object cco:PhysicalObject Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models tangible entities. Process cco:Process Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models activities or events. Event cco:Event Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models specific occurrences. Quality cco:Quality Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models attributes or properties of entities. Location cco:Location edr:Location Similar Both model spatial regions or places. Spatial Region cco:SpatialRegion edr:SpatialExtent Similar Both model spatial areas. Temporal Region cco:TemporalRegion edr:TemporalExtent Similar Both model time intervals. Parameter cco:Parameter edr:Parameter Similar Both model measurable properties. Information Object cco:InformationObject Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models data or representations. Dataset cco:Dataset edr:Dataset Similar Both model collections of data. Measurement cco:Measurement Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models quantified observations. Data Query Not explicitly modeled edr:DataQuery Narrower in EDR EDR focuses on data retrieval requests. Properties/Relationships hasQuality cco:hasQuality Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO links entities to their qualities. locatedIn cco:locatedIn edr:hasLocation Similar Both link entities to locations. participatesIn cco:participatesIn Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO links entities to processes. hasParameter cco:hasParameter edr:hasParameter Similar Both link processes or queries to parameters. hasPart cco:hasPart Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO links entities to their components. hasTemporalRegion cco:hasTemporalRegion edr:hasTemporalExtent Similar Both link entities to time intervals. hasValue cco:hasValue edr:hasValue Similar Both link measurements or parameters to values. hasUnit cco:hasUnit edr:hasUnit Similar Both link measurements or parameters to units. hasOutput cco:hasOutput Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO links processes to their results. Spatial/Temporal Types Point cco:Point edr:Point Similar Both model point geometries. Line cco:Line edr:Line Similar Both model line geometries. Polygon cco:Polygon edr:Polygon Similar Both model polygon geometries. Instant cco:Instant Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models specific points in time. Interval cco:Interval Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models time intervals with start and end points. Data and Measurements Information Object cco:InformationObject Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models data or representations. Measurement cco:Measurement Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models quantified observations. Dataset cco:Dataset edr:Dataset Similar Both model collections of data. Data Query Not explicitly modeled edr:DataQuery Narrower in EDR EDR focuses on data retrieval requests. Qualities and Parameters Quality cco:Quality Not explicitly modeled Broader in CCO CCO models attributes or properties of entities. Parameter cco:Parameter edr:Parameter Similar Both model measurable properties.

docs.title: 2.  Link/Bridge Concepts
docs.text:
The Link/bridge concepts in the shared ontology are used to align and integrate the Common Core Ontologies (CCO) and the OGC Environmental Data Retrieval (EDR). These bridge concepts ensure that the two ontologies can be interoperable. Table 4.2 shows the bridge relationships between CCO and EDR.

Table 2: Bridge concepts between CCO and EDR

Bridge Concept CCO Concept OGC EDR Concept Remarks EnvironmentalData cco:InformationContentEntity edr:EnvironmentalData Represents environmental data. Sensor cco:Device edr:Sensor Represents a device that measures environmental data. Observation cco:Process edr:Observation Represents the act of observing environmental data. FeatureOfInterest cco:Object edr:FeatureOfInterest Represents the entity being observed. Measurement cco:QualityValue edr:Measurement Represents a quantitative value of an observation. Location cco:SpatialLocation edr:Location Represents a spatial location. Time cco:TemporalLocation edr:Time Represents a temporal location. hasLocation cco:hasSpatialLocation edr:hasLocation Links an entity to its spatial location. hasTime cco:hasTemporalLocation edr:hasTime Links an entity to its temporal location. observes cco:performs edr:observes Links a sensor to the observation it performs.

Using the bridge concepts and the concept mappings described above the shared ontology is shown below.

docs.title: 3. Shared Ontology (ccoedr):
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<rdf:RDF xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#"
         xmlns:owl="http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#"
         xmlns:rdfs="http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#"
         xmlns:cco="http://www.ontologyrepository.com/CommonCoreOntologies/"
         xmlns:edr="http://www.opengis.net/ont/edr#"
         xmlns:ccoedr="http://www.example.org/ccoedr#">

  <!-- Shared Classes -->
  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;SpatialRegion">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;SpatialRegion"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;SpatialExtent"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Location">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Location"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;Location"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Parameter">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Parameter"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;Parameter"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;TemporalRegion">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;TemporalRegion"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;TemporalExtent"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Dataset">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Dataset"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;Dataset"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <!-- Broader CCO Classes (Not in EDR) -->
  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Process">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Process"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Event">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Event"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Quality">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Quality"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Measurement">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Measurement"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <!-- Narrower EDR Classes (Not in CCO) -->
  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;DataQuery">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;DataQuery"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <!-- Shared Properties -->
  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasLocation">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="cco;locatedIn"/>
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="edr;hasLocation"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasParameter">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="cco;hasParameter"/>
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="edr;hasParameter"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasTemporalExtent">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="cco;hasTemporalRegion"/>
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="edr;hasTemporalExtent"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <!-- Broader CCO Properties (Not in EDR) -->
  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasQuality">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="cco;hasQuality"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;participatesIn">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="cco;participatesIn"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasOutput">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="cco;hasOutput"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <!-- Narrower EDR Properties (Not in CCO) -->
  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasValue">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="edr;hasValue"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasUnit">
    <rdfs:subPropertyOf rdf:resource="edr;hasUnit"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <!-- Spatial/Temporal Types -->
  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Point">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Point"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;Point"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Line">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Line"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;Line"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Polygon">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Polygon"/>
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="edr;Polygon"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <!-- Broader CCO Temporal Types -->
  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Instant">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Instant"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <owl:Class rdf:about="ccoedr;Interval">
    <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="cco;Interval"/>
  </owl:Class>

  <!-- Axioms for Reasoning -->
  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasOutput">
    <owl:propertyChainAxiom rdf:parseType="Collection">
      <rdf:Description rdf:about="ccoedr;hasOutput"/>
      <rdf:Description rdf:about="ccoedr;retrieves"/>
    </owl:propertyChainAxiom>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;measures">
    <owl:inverseOf rdf:resource="ccoedr;hasParameter"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;hasParameter">
    <owl:propertyChainAxiom rdf:parseType="Collection">
      <rdf:Description rdf:about="ccoedr;hasParameter"/>
      <rdf:Description rdf:about="ccoedr;measures"/>
    </owl:propertyChainAxiom>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

  <owl:ObjectProperty rdf:about="ccoedr;retrieves">
    <owl:inverseOf rdf:resource="ccoedr;hasOutput"/>
  </owl:ObjectProperty>

</rdf:RDF>

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Cross-community data sharing is crucial: Defense/Intelligence (DoD/IC) and civilian sectors increasingly rely on each other's geospatial data for disaster response and emergency management.
  • Interoperability challenges: Significant hurdles exist in integrating data due to varying data sources, models, and updating frequencies.
  • Semantic heterogeneity is a major obstacle: Different organizations use different ontologies and standards to represent data, making it difficult to understand and combine information.

Need for a shared ontology: A common "reference ontology" is required to bridge the semantic gap and enable seamless data exchange between diverse organizations.

In essence: The text highlights the critical need for improved interoperability between geospatial data systems used by different sectors to effectively respond to disasters. This requires addressing the semantic challenges arising from diverse data representations.

docs.title: Potential Enhancement:
docs.text: • "A successful shared ontology will enable more efficient and effective disaster response by facilitating seamless data sharing and analysis across diverse organizations."

docs.title: Understanding the Terminology of the Representations and Key Steps in Developing the Shared Ontology:
Overview
docs.text:
• OGC EDR focuses on retrieving environmental data, describing spatial-temporal metadata, and access patterns.
  • CCO is designed for general-purpose use across domains, emphasizing logical formalism and consistency for entities, processes, and roles.

docs.title: Environmental Entities
docs.text: Includes phenomena like weather, climate, water bodies, and ecological features.

docs.title: Spatio-Temporal Aspects
docs.text: Both representations address time, location, and spatial geometries.

docs.title: Processes and Roles
docs.text:
• Processes: e.g., data retrieval, environmental phenomena.
  • Roles: e.g., data provider, data consumer.

docs.title: Identifying Similar Concepts and Bridging Classes/Properties for Alignment
docs.text:
• Use CCO’s upper ontology structure to align with EDR concepts, ensuring compatibility.
  • Define equivalence relationships (e.g., owl:equivalentClass or owl:equivalentProperty) for similar concepts.
  • Introduce bridge classes or properties where concepts and properties are narrower or broader.

docs.title: Development of a Mapping Framework Using RDF/OWL
docs.text: • SHACL Validation Schema

docs.title: Key Steps in Developing the Shared Ontology:
docs.text:
Concept Identification:

  • Environmental Entities: Identify and align concepts like weather, climate, water bodies, and ecological features from both OGC EDR and CCO.
  • Spatio-temporal: Recognize and harmonize how both systems represent time (edr:time ↔ cco:TimeInterval) and space (edr:geometry ↔ cco:SpatialRegion).
  • Processes and Roles: Align concepts related to data retrieval, environmental phenomena, and roles like data providers and consumers.

Shared Concepts and Harmonization:

  • Utilize CCO's Structure: Leverage the existing structure of CCO to align with EDR concepts, ensuring compatibility.
  • Define Equivalence: Establish clear equivalence relationships (e.g., owl:equivalentClass, owl:equivalentProperty) for concepts that are essentially the same in both systems.
  • Introduce Bridge Classes/Properties: For concepts that are narrower or broader in one system compared to the other, introduce bridge classes or properties to maintain consistency.

Ontology Creation Outline:

  • Metadata Structure: Map and align how environmental data formats, descriptions, and attributions are represented in both systems.
  • Spatio-temporal Dimensions: Integrate and harmonize the representations of temporal and spatial dimensions.
  • Entities and Phenomena: Align environmental entities (edr:DataEntity) with the entities and qualities defined within CCO.

Mapping Framework Development: Utilize RDF/OWL, a widely used language for representing knowledge in a machine-readable format, to create the formal mapping framework for the shared ontology.

docs.title: Table 1: Core Concepts in OGC EDR and their CCO Counterparts
docs.text: OGC EDR Concept Concept Definition CCO Remarks DataEntity Represents a data resource (e.g., dataset or observation). cco:PhysicalEntity Aligns environmental data with physical representations. Geometry Spatial description of the entity (e.g., bounding box, CRS). cco:SpatialRegion Use spatial definitions in CCO to describe extents. Time Temporal range of the dataset or event. cco:TimeInterval CCO’s temporal structure supports precise intervals. Parameter Describes the measured variables (e.g., temperature, humidity). cco:Quality Relates parameters to measurable qualities in CCO. CoverageType Type of coverage (e.g., point, trajectory, grid). Custom mapping via bridge classes Not directly in CCO, so bridge concepts are needed.

docs.title: Table 2: Selected mappings between EDR and CCO concepts
docs.text: OGC EDR Concept CCO Concept Mapping Example Feature of Interest (FOI) cco:SpatialRegion or cco:MaterialEntity Example: A lake (FOI) -> cco:SpatialRegion represents its geographical extent. Query (Spatial/Temporal) cco:Process Example: A temporal query to retrieve rainfall data -> cco:Process for data retrieval. Variable (e.g., temperature) cco:Attribute + cco:UnitOfMeasure Example: Temperature -> cco:Attribute with UnitOfMeasure in Celsius. Location (Coordinates) cco:Coordinate Example: A latitude-longitude point -> cco:Coordinate. Temporal Interval cco:TimeInterval Example: 2023-01-01T00:00Z to 2023-01-02T00:00Z -> cco:TimeInterval.

docs.title: Scope and Objectives:
docs.text:
• Approach for developing a shared vocabulary representation methods and specific metrics for the evaluation of the cross-walk mappings
  • Various metrics will be used to assess the depth of interoperability achieved.
  • Gap analysis based on expressivity of concepts that is required in disaster response and management activities and that which is possible using CCO and OGC APIs.
  • Identify elements that are not interoperable and elements that are ambiguous, i.e., could be mapped to multiple elements of the API content model or Common Core ontology

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: The DoD/IC has its own way of organizing data, while the OGC provides a set of rules to make it easier for different systems to share and use geospatial data, which is crucial for effective disaster response. The aim is to develop a mapping, making it more "FAIR" – Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable.

docs.title: Use Cases for Mapping OGC EDR API to Common Core Ontology (CCO)
docs.text: This document outlines three use cases that demonstrate how concepts from the OGC Environmental Data Retrieval (EDR) API can be mapped to the Common Core Ontology (CCO). These use cases involve semantic queries for flood-prone areas, temperature at a location, and average rainfall over a region.

docs.title: Use Case 1: Semantic Query for Flood-Prone Area
docs.text:
• Objective: To integrate flood-prone area data from the OGC Environment API with geospatial regions (e.g., hydrographic features) described in the CCO.
  • Query: Identify and retrieve flood-prone areas and their spatial links to hydrographic features (e.g., rivers, floodplains).
  • Key Concepts:
    • OGC EDR API:
      • FloodingLocation: Represents areas prone to flooding.
      • Geometry: Geospatial representation of flood-prone areas.
    • CCO Ontology:
      • HydrographicFeature: Represents water-related geographical entities like rivers, lakes, or basins.
      • SpatialPart: Links flood-prone areas to hydrographic features via spatial relationships.
  • Mappings:
    • OGC: FloodingLocation ↔ CCO: HydrographicFeature
    • OGC: Geometry ↔ CCO: SpatialPart
  • SPARQL Query (Illustrative):
    • The document includes a SPARQL query for retrieving data related to precipitation and soil saturation, although this query does not directly map flood-prone areas to hydrographic features.
    • The provided query looks for observations of precipitation within a date range and geospatial regions with soil saturation above 80%.
    • The query uses cco:Process for precipitation observations, cco:GeospatialRegion for spatial features, cco:has_spatial_part to link features with their coverage, and cco:attribute to specify the type of data. It also includes time filters and saturation value filters.
  • Mapped Concepts:
    • ogc:Observation → cco:Process
    • ogc:observedProperty → cco:attribute
    • ogc:hasTemporalExtent → cco:has_temporal_extent
    • ogc:startTime → cco:has_start_time
    • ogc:endTime → cco:has_end_time
    • ogc:Feature → cco:GeospatialRegion
    • ogc:hasCoverage → cco:has_spatial_part
    • ogc:observedProperty → cco:attribute
    • ogc:hasValue → cco:has_measurement_value

docs.title: Use Case 2: Temperature at a Location
docs.text:
• OGC EDR API Request: Retrieve the temperature at location (35.6895°N, 139.6917°E) at 2023-01-01T12:00Z.
  • Mapped CCO Concepts:
    • A cco:Process named :Request_001 has an input cco:SpatialRegion named :Location_001 and an output cco:Attribute named :Temperature_Reading_001, and occurs during the time interval :TimeInterval_2023-01-01_12:00Z.
    • The :Location_001 has coordinates of latitude "35.6895" and longitude "139.6917", linked through a cco:Coordinate named :Coordinate_Tokyo.
    • The :Temperature_Reading_001 has a value of "15.2" with a unit of measure in Celsius.

docs.title: Use Case 3: Average Rainfall Over a Region
docs.text:
• OGC EDR API Request: Retrieve the average rainfall in a bounding box region for the week of 2023-06-01 to 2023-06-07.
  • Mapped CCO Concepts:
    • A cco:Process named :Request_002 has an input cco:SpatialRegion named :Region_BBox_001 and an output cco:Attribute named :Rainfall_Statistic_001, and occurs during the time interval :TimeInterval_2023-06.
    • The :Region_BBox_001 is defined by a bounding box :BBox_Coordinates_001, which is a cco:SpatialRegion, with a lower-left coordinate :Coordinate_LowerLeft (30.0, -100.0) and an upper-right coordinate :Coordinate_UpperRight (40.0, -90.0).
    • The :Rainfall_Statistic_001 has a value of "102.3" with a unit of measure in mm.

These use cases illustrate how various OGC EDR API concepts can be mapped to the CCO, enabling semantic interoperability and data integration across different systems. The use of cco:Process, cco:SpatialRegion, cco:Attribute, and related properties helps provide a structured way to represent environmental data and queries.

docs.title: Use Cases to Demonstrate the Usefulness of the Shared Ontology
docs.text: Below are use cases that demonstrate the use of the shared ontology to interoperate between the CCO and OGC EDR.

docs.title: Use Case 1: Rainfall Event Monitoring
docs.text:
Below is an example RDF data snippet capturing various details related to a rainfall event. 

@prefix rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> .  
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .  
@prefix ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr#> .  
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .  

# Rainfall Event  
<http://example.org/rainfall#RainfallEvent_2023>  
    a ccoedr:Process ;  
    rdfs:label "Rainfall Event 2023" ;  
    ccoedr:hasLocation <http://example.org/location#CityABC> ;  
    ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent <http://example.org/time#Interval_2023> ;  
    ccoedr:hasOutput <http://example.org/data#RainfallDataset> .  

# Location  
<http://example.org/location#CityABC>  
    a ccoedr:Location ;  
    rdfs:label "City ABC" ;  
    ccoedr:SpatialRegion <http://example.org/spatial#Region_CityABC> .  

# Spatial Region  
<http://example.org/spatial#Region_CityABC>  
    a ccoedr:SpatialRegion ;  
    rdfs:label "Spatial Region of City ABC" .  

# Temporal Region  
<http://example.org/time#Interval_2023>  
    a ccoedr:TemporalRegion ;  
    rdfs:label "September 1-7, 2023" ;  
    ccoedr:hasStartTime "2023-09-01T00:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime ;  
    ccoedr:hasEndTime "2023-09-07T23:59:59Z"^^xsd:dateTime .  

# Sensor  
<http://example.org/sensor#Sensor_002>  
    a ccoedr:PhysicalObject ;  
    rdfs:label "Rainfall Sensor 002" ;  
    ccoedr:locatedIn <http://example.org/location#CityABC> ;  
    ccoedr:measures <http://example.org/parameter#Rainfall> .  

# Parameter (Rainfall)  
<http://example.org/parameter#Rainfall>  
    a ccoedr:Parameter ;  
    rdfs:label "Rainfall" ;  
    ccoedr:hasUnit "millimeters" .  

# Dataset  
<http://example.org/data#RainfallDataset>  
    a ccoedr:Dataset ;  
    rdfs:label "Rainfall Dataset" ;  
    ccoedr:hasParameter <http://example.org/parameter#Rainfall> ;  
    ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent <http://example.org/time#Interval_2023> ;  
    ccoedr:hasLocation <http://example.org/location#CityABC> .  

# Data Query  
<http://example.org/query#RainfallQuery>  
    a ccoedr:DataQuery ;  
    rdfs:label "Rainfall Data Query" ;  
    ccoedr:hasParameter <http://example.org/parameter#Rainfall> ;  
    ccoedr:hasLocation <http://example.org/location#CityABC> ;  
    ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent <http://example.org/time#Interval_2023> ;  
    ccoedr:retrieves <http://example.org/data#RainfallDataset> .

docs.title: Query 1: Retrieve All Rainfall Data Sets
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>

SELECT ?dataset ?label
WHERE {
  ?dataset a ccoedr:Dataset ;
           rdfs:label ?label .
}

docs.title: Query 2: Retrieve All Sensors Measuring Rainfall
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>

SELECT ?sensor ?label
WHERE {
  ?sensor a ccoedr:PhysicalObject ;
          rdfs:label ?label ;
          ccoedr:measures <http://example.org/parameter#Rainfall> .
}

docs.title: Use Case 2: Flood Monitoring
docs.text:
Below is an example RDF data snippet capturing various details related to a flood event. 

@prefix rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> .
@prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
@prefix ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr#> .
@prefix xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> .
@prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .

# Flood Event
ex:flood#FloodEvent_2023 a ccoedr:Process ;
    rdfs:label "Flood Event 2023" ;
    ccoedr:hasLocation ex:location#RiverXYZ ;
    ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent ex:time#Interval_2023 ;
    ccoedr:hasOutput ex:data#WaterLevelDataset .

# Location
ex:location#RiverXYZ a ccoedr:Location ;
    rdfs:label "River XYZ" ;
    ccoedr:SpatialRegion ex:spatial#Region_RiverXYZ .

# Spatial Region
ex:spatial#Region_RiverXYZ a ccoedr:SpatialRegion ;
    rdfs:label "Spatial Region of River XYZ" .

# Temporal Region
ex:time#Interval_2023 a ccoedr:TemporalRegion ;
    rdfs:label "October 1-5, 2023" ;
    ccoedr:hasStartTime "2023-10-01T00:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime ;
    ccoedr:hasEndTime "2023-10-05T23:59:59Z"^^xsd:dateTime .

# Sensor
ex:sensor#Sensor_001 a ccoedr:PhysicalObject ;
    rdfs:label "Water Level Sensor 001" ;
    ccoedr:locatedIn ex:location#RiverXYZ ;
    ccoedr:measures ex:parameter#WaterLevel .

# Parameter (Water Level)
ex:parameter#WaterLevel a ccoedr:Parameter ;
    rdfs:label "Water Level" ;
    ccoedr:hasUnit "meters" .

# Dataset
ex:data#WaterLevelDataset a ccoedr:Dataset ;
    rdfs:label "Water Level Dataset" ;
    ccoedr:hasParameter ex:parameter#WaterLevel ;
    ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent ex:time#Interval_2023 ;
    ccoedr:hasLocation ex:location#RiverXYZ .

# Data Query
ex:query#WaterLevelQuery a ccoedr:DataQuery ;
    rdfs:label "Water Level Data Query" ;
    ccoedr:hasParameter ex:parameter#WaterLevel ;
    ccoedr:hasLocation ex:location#RiverXYZ ;
    ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent ex:time#Interval_2023 ;
    ccoedr:retrieves ex:data#WaterLevelDataset .

docs.title: Query 1: Retrieve All Flood Events with Their Locations
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>

SELECT ?event ?eventLabel ?location ?locationLabel
WHERE {
  ?event a ccoedr:Process ;
         rdfs:label ?eventLabel ;
         ccoedr:hasLocation ?location .
  ?location rdfs:label ?locationLabel .
}

docs.title: Query 2: Retrieve All Sensors and Their Measured Parameters
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>

SELECT ?sensor ?sensorLabel ?parameter ?parameterLabel
WHERE {
  ?sensor a ccoedr:PhysicalObject ;
          rdfs:label ?sensorLabel ;
          ccoedr:measures ?parameter .
  ?parameter rdfs:label ?parameterLabel .
}

docs.title: Query 3: Retrieve all flood events with their temporal extents
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr\#\>  
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema\#\>  
PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema\#\>

SELECT ?event ?eventLabel ?startTime ?endTime  
WHERE {  
  ?event a ccoedr:Process ;  
         rdfs:label ?eventLabel ;  
         ccoedr:hasTemporalExtent ?temporalExtent .  
  ?temporalExtent ccoedr:hasStartTime ?startTime ;  
                  ccoedr:hasEndTime ?endTime .  
}

docs.title: Query 4: Retrieve all sensors located in a specific region
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr\#\>  
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema\#\>

SELECT ?sensor ?sensorLabel  
WHERE {  
  ?sensor a ccoedr:PhysicalObject ;  
          rdfs:label ?sensorLabel ;  
          ccoedr:locatedIn <http://example.org/location\#RiverXYZ\> .  
}

docs.title: Query 5: Retrieve all datasets for a specific parameter (e.g., water level)
docs.text:
PREFIX ccoedr: <http://www.example.org/ccoedr\#\>  
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema\#\>

SELECT ?dataset ?datasetLabel  
WHERE {  
  ?dataset a ccoedr:Dataset ;  
           rdfs:label ?datasetLabel ;  
           ccoedr:hasParameter <http://example.org/parameter\#WaterLevel\> .  
}

docs.title: Datasources
docs.text: The virtual assistant leverages the following datasets: * Copernicus data sources * ECMWF Climate Data Store (CDS) * Green Deal Data Space * Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) * WEkEO Environmental Data Hub * Github Repository of WEkEO * Github Repository of ECMWF

docs.title: FAIR Evaluation
docs.text: The data for the projet is mainly obtained from the existing web sources such as websites and github repositories which are open and free and accessible by all. The virtual assitant is built utilising free and open source llm models. The assitant gives information about the sources which are FAIR complaint and hence adheres to FAIR standards.

docs.title: Findings and Lessons Learned
docs.text:
The assistant enhances the data search and provides an interactive way to explore and learn more about the data sources provided by Copernicus data stores.

The user asks questions to the assistant and the assistant can answer using two ways. The two approaches are described below:

  • First approach (Local Database):

    • Fetch data from various data sources
    • Index the data in Chroma vector db
    • Match the stored documents in database with the user query
    • Return top 5 matching documents
    • Using the 5 documents generate a response using LLM

  • Second approach (Web search):

    • For the given user query, find relevant web sources
    • Fetch the data from these sources and index into a temporary collection in the vector database
    • Match the query with the documents in database
    • Return the top 5 documents
    • Generate a response using LLM using the returned documents

The diagram below shows the two approaches as discussed above and the workflow.

The LLM model can be changed as per user choice and the available options are: - phi4:latest - llama 3.2:latest - llama 3.1:8b - llama3:latest - deepseek-r1:1.5b

All of the above are open sourced models and can be adopted for usage.

The main learnings of the process are outlined below:

  • The indexed data needs to be processed in a form of markdown which makes the indexing easier and in a way which LLMs can understand highlighting the need for a LLM friendly data format.
  • The data needs to be cleaned and then indexed, a lot of irrelevant or extra things will increase the total documents and increased time to find match
  • The local db search approach re-ranks the searched documents adopts BM25 algorithm
  • The response time in case of CPU is lot higher than the GPU response, hence scaling and providing more better results a GPU is necessity
  • The prompt given by user becomes very important for the case of web search

docs.title: Future Directions
docs.text:
We plan to enhance the assistant by:

  • Adding reasoning capabilities.
  • Implementing visualization tools for scientific output.
  • Extending support to more OGC standards.

docs.text:

docs.text:
Our project aims to:

  • Build a Generative AI-enabled virtual assistant.
  • Enhance data discoverability using NLP and structured APIs.
